focus: The small-team model: who can talk to, approve for and change a Bot, shared versus per-person memory, and the smallest sign-in and roles model for a few people on one machine or a shared host.
noveltyJustification: 8 of 10 findings were fully new and 2 synthesized the small-team model onto the existing OS-level state layout.
ruledOut: Building a password store or SSO for a few people
Sharing one memory file for everything

label: OpenBot's personal edition runs for one person on their own machine: nobody signs in, there is one computer, and the deployment starts with a single Personal Assistant Bot.
OpenBot's team edition adds one Everyone admin scope above Every Bot and This Bot; people, sign-in and policy are how an admin sets the eight primitives, not a ninth primitive.
OpenBot requires an identity provider, and its OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER escape hatch refuses to start on a public address because every visitor would be the administrator.
A routine runs as the person who created it, with that person's own grants, so a routine can do exactly what its creator could do in chat and nothing more.
OpenBot's memory scope follows origin: facts a person adds are shared with all their Bots, while facts a Bot learns stay with that Bot.
Skilled bots keys every label, queue, lease and state folder by repository identity, and keeps state a run must not write under a user-level root outside every checkout with owner-only permissions.

Skilled bots has no sign-in or roles: bots are files changed through git, so change authority is repository write access, and approval authority is whoever can read the user-level state root holding needs-you items.

The smallest one-machine model is no sign-in: the OS user plus repository write access is the role model, a team-wide shared memory file sits beside a per-bot file, and a per-person file lives in that user's state root. Size S, low risk.

The smallest shared-host model is OS users with 0700 state roots and a 0600 vault, plus an owner field in BOT.md naming who may change or approve that Bot; no password store, roles or SSO. A shared bearer token is only needed if a socket or web surface is added.

Enterprise SSO and the team admin policy layer belong on the skip list: OpenMausBot's enterprise/ is separately licensed, and OpenBot's team scope administers many people, which a few people on one machine do not need.
